card.hook: Picture a fortress with walls several metres thick, parked on a cliff where the Atlantic slams into the harbour entrance. El Morro looks very solid in a photo, and the sea is happy to help with the drama.
card.stand_here: Stand on Paseo del Morro, the paved walkway that runs along the sea wall up to the fort. The fort is to the east of you, so face that way and you'll see it close up from the water side, with the wall, the surf and the green slope together.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the fort. Go to 0.5x to squeeze the wall, surf and green slope into one frame. Try 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the lighthouse or the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the sea wall along a lower line so the fort rises above it, and keep the horizon level.
card.best_time: Sunset is the one, according to several guides, with good light and clean backgrounds. This walkway is also said to be quieter than the main lawn.
card.selfie_here: Head to the grassy lawn in front of the fort's main façade and face the ocean, so the fortress is behind you. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if your phone has it) and hold it a bit low so the walls and lighthouse fit over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Plaza del Quinto Centenario, where El Morro is in view, to take your photo with the fort behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Paseo del Morro is reported to be free to walk from the Paseo de la Princesa end, but one visitor review says entering from the fort side carries a fee. The fort's interior and ramparts close in the late afternoon, so check the official site before you go. One guide advises avoiding the La Perla neighborhood at night.
card.challenge: Take a quick burst of the surf hitting the wall, then pick the frame where the spray looks like it's trying to reach the fort.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1539 as a fortified tower, and by 1595 it had grown into a bastion fort. Work carried on for about two more centuries, and it reached its present form in 1787. The walls rise about 43 metres from the shoreline, and UNESCO listed the fort as a World Heritage Site in 1983.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Paseo del Morro, the paved walkway that runs along the sea wall up to the fort. The fort is to the east of you, so face that way and you'll see it close up from the water side, with the wall, the surf and the green slope together.

card.hook: Imagine a cobblestone street with no cars, colonial facades on both sides, and a pale palace waiting at the top. Some days there are umbrellas or kites floating overhead too.
card.stand_here: Stand at the lower end of Calle Fortaleza in Old San Juan and face uphill toward the governor's residence. The palace is about 430 m on foot, walking west and uphill.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole street with the palace at the top. Try 0.5x to fit in more facades and any decorations overhead, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the palace.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the buildings straight, then tap the palace and slide a little darker so the sky and the pale walls keep their detail.
card.best_time: Go in the morning or late afternoon, when the light is softer and there are fewer people. Early morning also helps you beat the cruise-day crowds.
card.selfie_here: Stay on the car-free cobblestones of Calle Fortaleza (Umbrella Street), which leads straight to the mansion. Use the front camera at 0.5x and put the palace and any decorations over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Walk northwest along the city wall from the La Rogativa statue to the Pink House, where the wall curves out toward the bay, and ask someone to shoot back toward La Fortaleza from the wall.
card.rules_and_safety: The street and the outside of the building are free to photograph, but you can only go inside on a guided tour. The decorations change often, and one reviewer found the umbrellas gone and the street barricaded, so check conditions before you go. San Juan heat can be intense, so carry water and spare batteries.
card.challenge: Take one photo with the palace dead centre at the top, then see if a friend can spot every decoration hanging above the street.
card.good_to_know: La Fortaleza, also called the Palacio de Santa Catalina, was built between 1533 and 1540 as a fortress. It was remodelled in 1846 into the Neoclassical palace you see today. It has housed the governor since the 16th century, which makes it the oldest executive mansion in continuous use in the Americas, and it was listed as a World Heritage Site in 1983.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the lower end of Calle Fortaleza in Old San Juan and face uphill toward the governor's residence. The palace is about 430 m on foot, walking west and uphill.

card.hook: Here's a beach where the best photo bomber has wings. Planes glide in low over the turquoise water, so a passing jet can be the star of your shot.
card.stand_here: Stand on Playa Isla Verde, about 320 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stay on the sand near the waterline and decide first whether you want planes or the beach and hotels.
card.zoom: Use zoom 0.5x for the long beach and the hotel skyline, and zoom 1x for planes over the sand. If your phone has zoom 2x-5x, it brings a plane closer, but keep some sky around it.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the horizon on the lower line, so two thirds of your photo is sky and a plane has room to cross it. Then tap the plane or the sky and drag the slider down a touch so the sky stays colourful.
card.best_time: Afternoon is best for planes over the beach. For the beach and hotel skyline in early sunlight, go in the early morning.
card.selfie_here: Try the Pine Grove end, on the sand at the free-access section at the eastern end of the beach. One guide describes it as quieter and greener, with less resort architecture in the background. Use the front camera, or zoom 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the beach behind your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: A travel guide says petty crime is a reality on San Juan beaches, so be careful if you're alone on the sand. Access routes, parking and hotel areas may have their own rules, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a plane crossing the sky with the horizon sitting on your lower gridline, and take a few shots because it's over in seconds.
card.good_to_know: Isla Verde means "green island" in Spanish, named after a small cay and reef a little way off the shore. The beach sits right next to Luis Muñoz Marín International Airport, which is why the planes fly so low. It's officially part of the municipality of Carolina, though it shares its coastline with Ocean Park and Condado, which are part of San Juan.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Playa Isla Verde, about 320 m south of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north. Stay on the sand near the waterline and decide first whether you want planes or the beach and hotels.

card.hook: Most people shoot Condado Beach standing up, and the sand ends up as a boring strip at the bottom. Get down low and the whole beach turns golden.
card.stand_here: Head to Avenida Ashford, where the beachfront hotel strip meets the sand, and step onto the beach. Face the hotels and crouch down so the mid-century facades line up behind you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the sand and the long line of hotels. Switch to 1x for a calmer, less stretched look at the facades. For one hotel or the bridge, try 2x to 5x from a safe distance, depending on your phone.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sky or the facades, then drag the slider to darker so the sand doesn't turn white.
card.best_time: Golden hour is the best moment here. Shoot from a low angle and the sand glows.
card.selfie_here: Find the Puerto Rican flag set up on the beach and pose with the sand and ocean behind you. Use the front camera, and check the Plus Code FW4H+WMH on your map first so you land in the right spot.
card.rules_and_safety: Waves can be stronger than they look, and winter swells (December to March) are larger. Check conditions first and keep your phone and your feet back from the shoreline.
card.challenge: Crouch low, turn on the gridlines and get the hotel facades dead level with the sand filling the bottom of the frame.
card.good_to_know: Condado Beach is a large public beach in the Condado district of Santurce, just east of the old islet of San Juan. It runs from La Ventana al Mar Park in the west to Punta Piedrita in the east. Behind it stand La Concha Resort, the San Juan Marriott and the historic Vanderbilt Hotel.

card.hook: Picture a tiny stone sentry box hanging off a cliff with nothing behind it but the Atlantic. That's the Garita del Diablo, the most photographed spot on the ocean side of Castillo San Cristóbal, and it's easy to see why.
card.stand_here: Head inside Castillo San Cristóbal and follow the ramparts on the Atlantic side. Stand on the rampart and turn around to look back at the sentry box, with the open sea filling the background.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so you get the whole sentry box against the sea. Then step back and try zoom 2x for a tighter, flatter view. Use zoom 0.5x only if you want the whole rampart and sweep of coast in the frame.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the sentry box, then drag the slider to a bit darker if the sky starts to wash out.
card.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds, gives you the best shot at empty ramparts. Check the official site for current opening hours before you go.
card.selfie_here: Look for the covered passage on your left as you enter, at the edge of the main plaza, right next to the old wagon. Use the front camera and keep the richly coloured, textured walls and the wagon behind you. For a moodier selfie, the Garita del Diablo above the rocky coastline works too, with the sentry box over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on Calle Norzagaray, facing the fort's front near the entrance ramp, while you stand in the foreground so the whole fort fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep well back from the edge and keep one hand firmly on your phone. One guide advises avoiding the La Perla neighbourhood at night; it lies on the northern side between El Morro and Castillo San Cristóbal.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the sentry box on a third of the frame and a perfectly level horizon, then try to beat it with a selfie where the sea looks just as straight.
card.good_to_know: Castillo San Cristóbal is the big stone fort on the Atlantic side of Old San Juan. The grounds, ramparts and sentry box are part of a ticketed National Park Service site, so plan to go in rather than shoot from outside. For a second picture, the fort also gives a wide view over the Old San Juan rooftops, the harbour and the Atlantic horizon. Plaza de Colón is free and shows the fort as a large stone mass at the end of the streets.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head inside Castillo San Cristóbal and follow the ramparts on the Atlantic side. Stand on the rampart and turn around to look back at the sentry box, with the open sea filling the background.

card.hook: Picture a big sculptural fountain in front of you, Victorian lampposts marching off into the distance, and centuries-old city walls running alongside. That's Paseo de la Princesa, and it photographs better than most postcards.
card.stand_here: Stand at the Fuente Raíces plaza, right at the Roots Fountain, and face back along the paseo toward the walls and the bay. The exact spot along the promenade isn't marked, so look for the big sculpture and you've found it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the fountain, the promenade and the walls into one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for sculpture figures or lampposts.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the horizon level, keep the fountain low in the frame, and let the trees and lampposts lead the eye down the paseo.
card.best_time: Sunset is the favourite, when the light on the fountain is at its warmest. On cruise-ship days it gets much busier around midday, so early or late gives you space for a clean shot.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the Raíces Fountain, with the bay in view behind you: use the front camera at 0.5x and tuck the sculpture over your shoulder. For a second selfie, try the Puerta de San Juan, standing under the archway so it frames the tree-lined promenade and lamps beyond.
card.ask_someone: Parque de las Palomas, on the hill above the paseo and a short uphill walk from the fountain, looks down over the promenade and fountain, so a helper could shoot from there while you pose below (check the hill's access first).
card.rules_and_safety: It's a public promenade with no entry requirement, but check the official site for events or closures before you go.
card.challenge: Get the fountain low in the frame and count how many lampposts you can fit leading off into the distance.
card.good_to_know: The promenade is about 0.8 km long and was built between 1852 and 1854. It's named for Princess Infanta Isabel, the first-born child of Queen Isabella II of Spain, and was restored in 1989. Fuente Raíces is by Luis Sanguino, dates from 1992, and celebrates the Taino, Spanish and Sub-Saharan African roots of Puerto Rican identity.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the Fuente Raíces plaza, right at the Roots Fountain, and face back along the paseo toward the walls and the bay. The exact spot along the promenade isn't marked, so look for the big sculpture and you've found it.

card.hook: A bright red gate in an old grey stone wall is about as easy as phone photography gets. Even a quick snap looks good, so you can relax and enjoy it.
card.stand_here: Head for Plazuela de la Rogativa, the small plaza on Caleta de las Monjas, about 70 m downhill to the south-east. Face the red gate, with the statue close to you in the foreground and the bay and walls beyond.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the gate, bay and walls in together. Switch to zoom 0.5x if you want the statue big in the foreground, and zoom 2x to make the red gate pop from the stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the gate on a lower intersection with the statue off to one side, then tap the red gate and slide it a touch darker so the red stays rich.
card.best_time: There's no official best time. Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the stone and the red paint than harsh midday sun, and one guide suggests arriving early because the streets get busy.
card.selfie_here: Walk through the arch, turn right onto the Paseo del Morro path on the bay side, and stand with the red gate behind you. Use the front camera at zoom 0.5x so the arch fits over your shoulder, and check the spot on arrival because it's based on general descriptions. Or step back inside the walls onto the colourful street and turn toward the gate.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Plazuela de la Rogativa, where the gate is in view, and take your photo with the gate in the shot.
card.rules_and_safety: You can't enter El Morro fort from outside the wall, and the gate-side path is short. One visitor found the walkway out over the beach closed, so check access before you head that way.
card.challenge: Take three frames from the same spot, one wide, one close on the gate and one with the statue as the star, then pick a winner.
card.good_to_know: San Juan Gate is the red gate set into the old stone city walls, with colonial buildings and the bay close by. The plaza is close to La Fortaleza and very near the gate. You only need a few minutes here.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Plazuela de la Rogativa, the small plaza on Caleta de las Monjas, about 70 m downhill to the south-east. Face the red gate, with the statue close to you in the foreground and the bay and walls beyond.

card.hook: Picture a bright white cathedral glowing at the end of a quiet colonial street, with nobody walking through your shot. That's Calle del Cristo if you show up early.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle del Cristo, on the stretch in front of the cathedral facade, about 1 minute on foot to the east of the cathedral's centre. Face east, toward the white front of the cathedral.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole height of the facade from the narrow street. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the doorway and upper facade.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white facade, then slide the brightness a little darker so the white stone keeps its detail, and turn on gridlines so the building doesn't lean.
card.best_time: Go early, between about 6:30 and 8:00 a.m. The street is quiet and the light is soft, so you can get a clean shot without strangers in it. Late in the afternoon the shadows can turn harsh.
card.selfie_here: Head to Plaza de la Catedral, the square directly across from the cathedral, so the church stands behind you. Use the front camera, hold it at arm's length, and try 0.5x to squeeze more of the facade over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in Plazuela Las Monjas, the shaded little park where the main entrance faces, and shoot toward the entrance while you stand in front of the church so the front fills the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a place of worship, so dress modestly and keep quiet during services. Services come first, so be discreet and ask before photographing people. Check the official site for visiting times and photography rules.

card.good_to_know: This is the oldest purpose-built cathedral still standing in the Americas. The first church here was wood, from 1513, but a hurricane destroyed it in 1529. card.hook: Leave El Morro, walk down the grassy slope, and the whole white cemetery suddenly appears with the blue Atlantic right behind it. It's a quiet, beautiful scene, and you get it all in one go.
card.stand_here: Stand on the grassy field at the exit of Castillo San Felipe del Morro and look down towards the cemetery. It's to the east, with the fort's walls close beside it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the cemetery, the sea and the fort walls together. Try 0.5x if you want more fort and sky, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the white tombs and walls.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white walls, then slide the brightness down a little so they keep their detail against the bright sky.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white walls than the middle of the day. Check which way the sun falls on the day you visit.
card.selfie_here: Head to the western part of the cemetery, where the coastline shows behind the tombs. Use the front camera at 0.5x, with the sea over your shoulder, and keep it low-key and respectful.

card.rules_and_safety: This is a working place of remembrance, so keep your voice down and stay on the paths. Photography is generally allowed, but respect any ceremonies, and check the official site for El Morro and cemetery visiting rules before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot at 0.5x and one at 1x from the same spot, then pick your winner later over a cold drink.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1863, and many of Puerto Rico's best-known writers, musicians, politicians and activists are buried here. The site was chosen to look out over the ocean, and the sea view was meant to symbolise the spirit's journey to the afterlife. The wall averages about 12 metres in height.

card.hook: Most people hit the straight-on view of San José Church and move on. Try the sneaky side angle first: the church squeezes in among the Old San Juan streets like it's part of the neighbourhood, because it is.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza del Quinto Centenario and face south-east, because the church is to the south-east of you. From here you get a side, three-quarter view with the town tucked around it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the three-quarter view. If the streets feel tight and the whole building won't fit, tap 0.5x. Zoom 2x or more (depends on your phone) is great for the doorway and the upper walls.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on your gridlines and line the church up along a vertical line so the walls don't lean, then tap the church and slide the brightness a touch darker to keep the stonework detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and gentler shadows on the walls than the middle of the day.
card.selfie_here: Head to Plaza San José and stand beside the Juan Ponce de León statue, by its garden area, so the church façade fills the background. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the paved open space around the statue's garden while you pose by the statue, with the church at the far end of the plaza behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The church doors have sometimes been found closed, so check opening hours before planning to go in. The views from the plazas don't depend on it being open.
card.challenge: Take the same church twice, once from the side in Plaza del Quinto Centenario and once across Plaza de San José, then see which one your friends like better.
card.good_to_know: San José Church was begun in 1528 and founded in 1532 as part of a Dominican convent dedicated to Thomas Aquinas. It's built in the Isabelline style, a blend of late Gothic and early Renaissance Spanish architecture. Juan Ponce de León, the first governor of Puerto Rico, was buried in its crypt from 1559 until 1836, and a long restoration finished in March 2021.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in Plaza del Quinto Centenario and face south-east, because the church is to the south-east of you. From here you get a side, three-quarter view with the town tucked around it.

card.hook: This chapel is tiny, and that's exactly why it works. One white bell tower, three wide arches, and the whole harbour waiting behind the city wall.

card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the chapel, bell tower and harbour in one shot. Tap 0.5x if you want more of the arches and the wall in a tight space, and 2x or more to pick out the belfry on its own.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white chapel wall, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and water keep their colour and the stone doesn't glare.
card.best_time: Go early. The street is reportedly busy by late morning, and the park is usually calmer than the street. Some guides also suggest the park at sunset.
card.selfie_here: Use the small paved terrace at the far end of Calle del Cristo, by Parque de las Palomas. Face the bay with the chapel behind you, use the front camera (try 0.5x to fit more in) and hold the phone a little higher than your face.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand higher up Calle del Cristo while you stand mid-street, so the chapel sits at the far end of the cobbles (before about 9 a.m. there are fewer people).
card.rules_and_safety: If you step inside, photography is generally fine, but be discreet, skip the flash and respect anyone praying. The chapel is reportedly open only on certain days. Wear comfortable shoes, because Old San Juan's streets are uneven and hilly.
card.challenge: Get all three arches in one frame, with the bell tower sitting neatly on a gridline.
card.good_to_know: Capilla del Cristo is an 18th-century Spanish Baroque chapel, and most of the objects on its altar date from 1753. The gate was added in the 1940s to protect the interior, and a volunteer brotherhood still looks after the building. Its front is a popular image on Puerto Rican travel guides and souvenirs, so it may look familiar.

card.hook: Picture a big white Roman temple with the Atlantic sparkling behind it. That's El Capitolio, and it's just outside the walls of Old San Juan, so it looks a little lost in the best way.
card.stand_here: Stand in Plaza San Juan Bautista, on the north side of the Capitol, and face the building. You'll get the white marble steps and columns with open sea and sky behind them, the classic postcard view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole wide frontage in. If it won't fit, try 0.5x and keep the Capitol in the middle so the edges don't bend. Then zoom 2x or more for the columns and the dome.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line up the middle of the columns with the centre of the screen, and tap the white marble, then slide it a touch darker so the stone keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the white marble. The front faces north, so check where the sun is on the day.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera on Plaza San Juan Bautista, across the street from the Capitol's north side, and step back so the building sits over your shoulder. Try 0.5x to squeeze in more of it. The Paseo de los Presidentes, with its bronze presidents in all sorts of poses, is a fun second spot directly across from the Capitol.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on the Paseo de los Presidentes walkway, across Constitution Avenue from the Capitol, and stand in front of the building so they can step back and fit it all in.
card.rules_and_safety: You can photograph the outside and the plaza from outside. The interior may close during legislative sessions or construction, and tour access can be limited, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Keep the horizon dead level and get the steps, columns and sea all in one shot. Gridlines make it easy, so no wonky Roman temples allowed.
card.good_to_know: El Capitolio is the seat of Puerto Rico's Legislative Assembly. It was built between 1921 and 1929 in a Neoclassical Beaux-Arts style, and architect Rafael Carmoega designed it to resemble the Pantheon in Rome. It has been on the U.S. National Register of Historic Places since 1977.

card.hook: Casa Blanca was built for Juan Ponce de León, and he never spent a night in it. The pale walls look great against the bay, so you get to enjoy the view he missed.
card.stand_here: Stand on Paseo del Morro, on the bay side of the house. From there the house is to the north-east, about 1 minute on foot, so turn and look back toward its southwest side with the water and the old city wall beside it.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to fit the whole house, the bay and the wall in one frame. Try 0.5x if you want more sky and water, then 2x or more (depends on your phone) for windows, walls and terraces.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the white walls, then slide the brightness down a little (darker) so they keep their detail against the sky.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light flatters the white walls. A clear sky makes the bay stand out too.
card.selfie_here: Try the back garden by the fountain. Walk to the end of Calle San Sebastián to reach it, then use the front camera with the greenery and the house walls behind you. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the garden in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on Calle del Sol and step back along the street until the whole southeast side of the house fits, while you stand in front of the house.
card.rules_and_safety: Paseo del Morro is a public path, but the house and garden are part of a museum. Check the official site before you go for what's open and any entry rules.
card.challenge: Take three shots in a few minutes: one wide from Paseo del Morro, one straight-on from Calle del Sol, and one close-up of a wall or terrace. Then pick your favourite.
card.good_to_know: Building began in 1521. It later became the first governor's residence in Puerto Rico, with solid walls and terraces for guards and artillery. Today it's a house museum run by the Institute of Puerto Rican Culture, with 16th- and 17th-century objects inside and a garden with fountains.

card.hook: Picture a row of bright houses tumbling down a slope, a basketball court in the middle, and the Atlantic filling the top of your screen. You get all of it from the pavement, without taking a single step down.
card.stand_here: Stand on Calle Norzagaray, on the wall-side walkway above La Perla. Face down the slope, with the houses and the court below you and the sea beyond.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the houses, the court and the sea in one frame. Then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out the court or a patch of colour. Zoom 0.5x gives you more sea and sky, but keep the wall edge out of the corners.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and put the court or the row of houses on a lower line with the sea along the top third, then tap the brightest houses and slide it a little darker so the colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go in daylight, which is what the guides advise. Soft morning or late-afternoon light usually shows the colours best.
card.selfie_here: Take your selfie on Calle Norzagaray beside the colourful basketball court at the edge of the neighbourhood. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the court over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Try the wall walk between Castillo San Cristóbal and Plaza del Quinto Centenario, where La Perla is photographed from above: ask a passer-by to stand on the walkway and shoot back at you while you stand at the wall with the neighbourhood behind you (check the spot on site).
card.rules_and_safety: People live here, so photograph the murals, the coast and the views, and don't photograph residents or their homes without permission. Stay on the street above rather than going into the neighbourhood, skip the drone, and stop somewhere safe before you raise your phone, because the pavement has traffic and steep sections.
card.challenge: Can you get the court, the colourful houses and the line of the coast into one frame without a single person in it?
card.good_to_know: La Perla is a residential community on the slope below the old city wall, running down towards the Atlantic. Calle Norzagaray runs along the wall above it, on the way to the forts. If you're heading on, Castillo San Cristóbal gives you a second angle, with La Perla's roofs below the wall and the El Morro lighthouse in the distance.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Calle Norzagaray, on the wall-side walkway above La Perla. Face down the slope, with the houses and the court below you and the sea beyond.

card.hook: Plaza de Armas has already done the styling for you: pastel buildings, curved arcades and a fountain parked right in front like a prop. All you have to do is stand in the right spot and press the button.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon in the centre of the plaza, right beside the fountain. Face the buildings around the edge so the fountain fills the bottom of your shot and the colourful facades sit behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for the fountain with the facades behind it. Switch to 0.5x if you want more of the arcades and buildings squeezed in. Try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the bronze statue or for details on the facades.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines so the buildings stay straight, and put the fountain in the lower part of the frame.
card.best_time: Early morning is calmer, with soft light and fewer people. In the evening the plaza lights come on and a human statue often performs by the fountain, which is fun but means more people in your frame.
card.selfie_here: Head to the bench by the bronze statue of the salsa composer Tito Curet Alonso, inside the plaza, and sit on or beside it. It's a popular photo stop, so use the front camera and try 0.5x to fit more in.
card.ask_someone: Ask your helper to stand back across the plaza while you stand by the central fountain, so the fountain and the pastel facades fit in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: It's an open public plaza, but check locally for events before you go.
card.challenge: Guides say the fountain has four statues for the seasons, so see if you can get your favourite one in the shot with a pastel building behind it.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de Armas is a colonial square in San Juan, surrounded by pastel colonial buildings and arcades. Guides mention four statues on the fountain representing the seasons. On the first Saturday of the month there are bomba performances in the plaza, which can block your view, so be patient or shuffle a few steps to find a clear gap.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon in the centre of the plaza, right beside the fountain. Face the buildings around the edge so the fountain fills the bottom of your shot and the colourful facades sit behind it.

card.hook: Picture Columbus on top of a tall column, with a ring of colourful colonial buildings behind him like a painted stage set. It's a small square, but it's a busy one, with vendors and a line of people waiting for their selfie.
card.stand_here: Stand at the base of the Columbus monument in the centre of Plaza de Colón, right where the phone icon sits, so there's no extra walk once you're in the plaza. Face the statue and let the coloured buildings fill in behind it.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the column and the buildings together. If the square is packed and you need the whole column from close up, try zoom 0.5x. To pick the statue out against the sky, go to zoom 2x or higher (the higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line the column up with a vertical line so it stands straight, then tap the statue and slide it a little darker if the sky is bright.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning, before the tour groups and vendors arrive, for a clearer view and fewer people in your shot. The side of the square opposite the blue Antiguo Casino is open to the morning sun.
card.selfie_here: Head to the I Love SJ sign near the Columbus column. It's the plaza's classic photo stop, and you may find a few people queuing. Use your front camera and try stepping to a spot where the column peeks over your shoulder. The benches and small fountain area around the statue are another good place for a picture.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Calle O'Donnell side, across the street from the plaza, while you stand by the statue; it's worth a quick check on the map that the angle works.
card.challenge: Take your best photo of the column standing perfectly straight on a gridline, with not a single stranger in it. Take a few in a row and keep the cleanest.
card.good_to_know: Plaza de Colón is an open public square in San Juan, with a statue of Columbus on a tall column in the middle. For a second view, photograph the blue Antiguo Casino across the plaza, with the stone fort of San Cristóbal in the distance to the north-east.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the base of the Columbus monument in the centre of Plaza de Colón, right where the phone icon sits, so there's no extra walk once you're in the plaza. Face the statue and let the coloured buildings fill in behind it.

card.hook: Water on both sides, a bridge pointing your eye straight at an old fort, and a little sandy beach to stand on. Not a bad start to a walk.
card.stand_here: Head for Playita del Condado, the small sandy beach beside the road where the bridge begins at the Condado end. If you're coming along the shore, walk west to reach it, then face across the lagoon so the start of the bridge sits in front of you and the fort is in the distance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the beach, lagoon and bridge into one frame. Then try 1x for a more natural look, and 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull the fort in across the water.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the bridge along the lower third line, with the lagoon below and the fort and sky above.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives softer light. It's also much nicer to stand around then, because the bridge has very little shade.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera at 0.5x, hold your phone a little higher than your face, and turn so the bridge and lagoon fill the space over your shoulder. Take a few and pick the one where the bridge isn't cut off.
card.rules_and_safety: The bridge has little shade, so wear sunscreen and bring a hat and water. The Fortín de San Jerónimo may have restricted access or be closed for works, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take three quick shots in a row: wide, normal, then zoomed in on the fort. See which one you'd actually send to your friends.
card.good_to_know: Dos Hermanos means "Two Brothers". The bridge was designed and built by the brothers Hernand and Sosthenes Behn and opened on 22 May 1910. The Behns were also behind the Condado development, and the bridge helped make it reachable. It was rebuilt and restored, and the new bridge was inaugurated in December 2011.
